- tigris: Tigris object storage CLI reference. Use when working with object storage, file uploads, S3-compatible buckets, or blob storage. Provides commands, conventions, and environment setup for using Tigris via the tigris (t3) CLI.

- vercel:env: Manage Vercel environment variables. Commands include list, pull, add, remove, and diff. Use to sync environment variables between Vercel and your local development environment.
- vercel:status: Show the status of the current Vercel project — recent deployments, linked project info, and environment overview.
- vercel:access-protected-vercel-deployment: Access and test Vercel deployments protected by Vercel Authentication, SSO, or Deployment Protection. Use when curl, agent-browser, Playwright, or another automated request reaches a Vercel login or protection page; when a protected preview or production URL returns 401 or 403; when TRUSTED_SOURCES_ENVIRONMENT_MISMATCH appears; or when choosing between `vercel curl` and the `x-vercel-trusted-oidc-idp-token` header.
- vercel:ai-gateway: Vercel AI Gateway guidance for setup, model discovery, authentication, routing, fallbacks, BYOK, budgets, spend reporting, observability, compatible APIs, and coding-agent configuration. Use when adding AI Gateway to an app, migrating provider calls, choosing models or providers, debugging gateway requests, or running `vercel ai-gateway` commands.
- vercel:ai-sdk: Vercel AI SDK expert guidance. Use when building AI-powered features — chat interfaces, text generation, structured output, tool calling, agents, MCP integration, streaming, embeddings, reranking, image generation, or working with any LLM provider.
- vercel:auth: Authentication integration guidance — Clerk (native Vercel Marketplace), Descope, and Auth0 setup for Next.js applications. Covers middleware auth patterns, sign-in/sign-up flows, and Marketplace provisioning. Use when implementing user authentication.

- vercel:cdn-caching: Debug Vercel CDN caching — cache hit rate, stale content, revalidation behavior, ISR + PPR, per-request cache reasons (cacheReason) and PPR state (ppr_state), and costs.
- vercel:chat-sdk: Vercel Chat SDK expert guidance. Use when building multi-platform chat bots — Slack, Telegram, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Google Chat, GitHub, Linear — with a single codebase. Covers the Chat class, adapters, threads, messages, cards, modals, streaming, state management, and webhook setup.
- vercel:create-a-backend: Backend architecture guidance. Use when planning, building, or migrating an API or backend; choosing between Functions, Services, containers, Workflow, Queues, and Marketplace databases; or selecting a supported backend framework or runtime.
- vercel:deployments-cicd: Vercel deployment and CI/CD expert guidance. Use when deploying, promoting, rolling back, inspecting deployments, building with --prebuilt, or configuring CI workflow files for Vercel.
- vercel:env-vars: Vercel environment variable expert guidance. Use when working with .env files, vercel env commands, OIDC tokens, or managing environment-specific configuration.
- vercel:eve: eve framework guidance for durable AI agents and agent-powered applications. Use when creating, editing, or debugging an eve project, when the user explicitly asks for eve, or when the build-agents skill has selected eve as the default framework. Covers eve's filesystem-first runtime, durable sessions, tools, skills, connections, channels, sandboxes, subagents, schedules, evals, frontend clients, and Agent Runs observability. Do not use for incidental agent mentions, generic agent-building prompts, or established non-eve stacks unless the user asks for comparison or migration.
- vercel:flags-sdk: Set up and use feature flags and A/B tests with the Flags SDK (`flags` npm package) and Vercel Flags. Use when installing or configuring the SDK, adding a new or existing flag, wiring `vercelAdapter` (OIDC or SDK keys), declaring flags with `flag()`, using the `vercel flags` CLI (create, inspect, list, enable, disable, set, update, split, rollout, rules, segments, use-targeting, evaluations, versions, open, archive, unarchive, rm, sdk-keys, override, prepare), setting up providers/adapters (Vercel, Statsig, LaunchDarkly, PostHog, GrowthBook, Global Config, OpenFeature, Split, Flagsmith, Reflag, Optimizely, or custom), precompute, `identify`/`dedupe`, Flags Explorer/Toolbar, Next.js or SvelteKit, or encrypting flag values. You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

1	# Releasing — versioning & CI
2	
3	Desktop (macOS Tauri app, auto-updates in-app) and mobile (React Native /
4	Expo) releases are **tag-driven** and intentionally separate.
5	
6	- The **git tag is the release trigger and the source of truth for the version.**
7	  You don't have to commit a version bump — tagging *is* the release. CI reads the
8	  version out of the tag and writes it into the app config before building. (The
9	  version committed in the repo is just the dev baseline.)
10	- See also: [DESKTOP_AUTO_UPDATE.md](./DESKTOP_AUTO_UPDATE.md) for the desktop
11	  updater internals, and [UPDATER_KEY_ROTATION.md](./UPDATER_KEY_ROTATION.md)
12	  for generating or rotating the signing key.
13	- For future Mac App Store / TestFlight releases, see
14	  [MACOS_APP_STORE_TESTFLIGHT.md](./MACOS_APP_STORE_TESTFLIGHT.md).
15	
16	---
17	
18	## 1. Versioning model
19	
20	**Separate tag namespaces.** Desktop and mobile can move independently:
21	
22	```
23	desktop-v0.5.0   desktop 0.5.0
24	mobile-v0.2.0    mobile 0.2.0
25	desktop-v0.5.1   desktop 0.5.1
26	```
27	
28	> Why GitHub's *latest* release matters for the updater: the desktop updater
29	> reads `…/releases/latest/download/latest.json`, so the desktop release must be
30	> marked as GitHub's latest release. The desktop workflow forces the `latest`
31	> flag on every desktop release. Mobile releases are also listed on GitHub,
32	> but are explicitly prevented from replacing the latest desktop release.
33	
34	---
35	
36	## 2. How to cut a desktop release
37	
38	### Option A — push a tag (normal path)
39	
40	```bash
41	git checkout main && git pull          # release from main
42	npm version 0.5.0 --no-git-tag-version  # optional: keep repo baseline in sync
43	git commit -am "Release 0.5.0" || true
44	
45	git tag desktop-v0.5.0
46	git push origin desktop-v0.5.0
47	```
48	
49	CI ([`.github/workflows/release.yml`](../.github/workflows/release.yml)) builds
50	the `.dmg` + updater artifacts and publishes the GitHub Release.
51	
52	### Option B — manual run (no tag)
53	
54	Actions tab → **Desktop Release** → **Run workflow** → enter the version.
55	Useful for re-running a failed build.
56	
57	### Option C — build locally
58	
59	CI is not rationed here: `oogxdd/type` is public, and GitHub Actions is free on
60	standard runners for public repositories. Build locally for *speed*, not cost —
61	a cold CI build takes 8–10 minutes, while your Mac rebuilds incrementally in
62	about two:
63	
64	```bash
65	# desktop needs the updater signing key in the environment:
66	export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY="$(cat ~/.tauri/type-updater.key)"
67	export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD="<password>"
68	
69	apps/desktop/scripts/release-local.sh 0.5.0
70	```
71	
72	It bumps the version, builds, signs, assembles `latest.json`, and creates the
73	GitHub Release via `gh` — exactly what CI does. (`gh auth login` required once.)
74	
75	---
76	
77	## 2b. Developing locally without touching the installed prod app
78	
79	The released app and a local dev build are **fully separate installs with
80	separate data**, as long as you use the dev config. Never point a dev run at the
81	production identifier — `com.digital.type2`'s app-data directory is where the
82	real notes live.
83	
84	| | Production | Dev |
85	| --- | --- | --- |
86	| Bundle | `/Applications/Type.app` | `/Applications/Type Dev.app` |
87	| Identifier | `com.digital.type2` | `com.digital.type2.dev` |
88	| App data (notes, profiles, keys) | `~/Library/Application Support/com.digital.type2` | `~/Library/Application Support/com.digital.type2.dev` |
89	| Auto-update | on (GitHub `latest.json`) | off (`endpoints: []`) |
90	
91	Everything above the identifier line is driven by
92	`apps/desktop/src-tauri/tauri.dev.conf.json`, which Tauri deep-merges over
93	`tauri.conf.json`.
94	
95	```bash
96	npm run desktop:app       # dev run against the dev identifier — safe
97	npm run desktop:dmg:dev   # "Type Dev.dmg", installs alongside prod
98	```
99	
100	`npm run desktop:app:prod-data` exists as an explicit escape hatch: it runs the
101	dev build against the **production** app-data directory. Use it only when you
102	deliberately need to reproduce something against real notes, and back up first
103	(see below).
104	
105	The dev config sets `plugins.updater.endpoints: []`, so a dev build can never
106	download and overwrite itself with a production release. The updater errors with
107	`EmptyEndpoints` if you press "Check for updates" there — that is intended.
108	
109	### Backing up production data
110	
111	Everything the desktop app owns lives under one directory:
112	
113	```bash
114	STAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
115	rsync -aH --exclude 'whisper/' --exclude '.DS_Store' \
116	  "$HOME/Library/Application Support/com.digital.type2/" \
117	  "/Volumes/KINGSTON/Backups/type/prod-$STAMP/app-data/"
118	ditto /Applications/Type.app "/Volumes/KINGSTON/Backups/type/prod-$STAMP/Type.app"
119	```
120	
121	`whisper/` is excluded because the managed Python env re-provisions itself.
122	Everything that matters — `notes/`, `profiles/`, `config.json`,
123	`.notes-profiles.json`, `local_sync/` — is a few tens of MB.
124	
125	---
126	
127	## 3. How to cut a mobile release
128	
129	For the native Xcode ad-hoc build, signing, and OTA deployment used by the
130	GitHub-hosted macOS runner, see
131	[MOBILE_AD_HOC_GITHUB_ACTIONS.md](./MOBILE_AD_HOC_GITHUB_ACTIONS.md).
132	
133	```bash
134	git checkout main && git pull
135	git tag mobile-v0.2.0
136	git push origin mobile-v0.2.0
137	```
138	
139	CI ([`.github/workflows/mobile-adhoc.yml`](../.github/workflows/mobile-adhoc.yml)):
140	
141	1. creates a GitHub Release without changing the desktop Latest,
142	2. runs on a macOS runner,
143	3. generates the iOS UniFFI/native module from `packages/mobile-core`,
144	4. archives and exports an ad-hoc `.ipa` with Xcode,
145	5. verifies its signature, version, and registered-device profile,
146	6. uploads it as a workflow artifact and tagged GitHub Release asset, and
147	7. deploys the OTA install site to `https://type-ota.vercel.app`.
148	
149	The workflow sets `MOBILE_VERSION` from the tag and uses the GitHub run number
150	as `IOS_BUILD_NUMBER`. For a manual run, use Actions → **Mobile Ad Hoc** and
151	optionally enter an explicit build number. Manual dispatch updates the OTA site
152	and keeps the IPA as a 30-day workflow artifact but does not create a GitHub
153	Release; the `github-release` job runs only for a pushed `mobile-v*` tag.
154	
155	---
156	
157	## 4. Required GitHub secrets
158	
159	Add under **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions**.
160	
161	### Mobile (required)
162	
163	The `ios` job keeps using the existing `testflight` GitHub Environment so its
164	Apple API-key secrets remain available; the legacy environment name does not
165	mean the workflow uploads to TestFlight. Add the following as environment
166	secrets (or repository secrets if environment scoping is not desired):
167	
168	| Secret | What it is |
169	| --- | --- |
170	| `APPLE_TEAM_ID` | Apple Developer team ID |
171	| `APP_STORE_CONNECT_KEY_ID` | Team App Store Connect API key ID |
172	| `APP_STORE_CONNECT_ISSUER_ID` | Team App Store Connect API issuer ID |
173	| `APP_STORE_CONNECT_PRIVATE_KEY` | Complete contents of the API key `.p8` file |
174	| `IOS_DISTRIBUTION_CERTIFICATE_BASE64` | Base64-encoded Apple Distribution `.p12` including its private key |
175	| `IOS_DISTRIBUTION_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | Password for that `.p12` |
176	| `IOS_AD_HOC_DEVICE_UDIDS` | Required registered device UDIDs, separated by commas, spaces, or newlines |
177	| `VERCEL_TOKEN` | Token with deploy access to the OTA project |
178	
179	`IOS_AD_HOC_BASE_URL`, `VERCEL_ORG_ID`, and `VERCEL_PROJECT_ID` are optional
180	repository variables. The workflow defaults them to the existing production
181	URL and Vercel project.
182	
183	The runner imports the distribution identity into a temporary Keychain; Xcode
184	uses the API key for automatic provisioning and exports with
185	`ExportOptionsAdHoc.plist`. Expo/EAS and TestFlight are not used. See
186	[MOBILE_AD_HOC_GITHUB_ACTIONS.md](./MOBILE_AD_HOC_GITHUB_ACTIONS.md) for setup.
187	
188	### Desktop (required)
189	
190	| Secret                                | What it is                                            |
191	| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
192	| `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY`           | Contents of `~/.tauri/type-updater.key`               |
193	| `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD`  | Password for that key                                 |
194	
195	`GITHUB_TOKEN` is provided automatically (used to create the Release).
196	
197	### Desktop — Apple notarization (optional)
198	
199	Without these the `.dmg` still works but triggers the "unidentified developer"
200	warning on first open. With them, tauri-action notarizes automatically:
201	`APPLE_CERTIFICATE`, `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD`, `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY`,
202	`APPLE_ID`, `APPLE_PASSWORD`, `APPLE_TEAM_ID`.
203	
204	Set **all six or none** — a partially configured setup fails the release rather
205	than falling back to unsigned. Full walkthrough, including the microphone
206	entitlement the hardened runtime requires:
207	[MACOS_CODE_SIGNING.md](./MACOS_CODE_SIGNING.md).
208	
209	---
210	
211	## 5. First-release checklist (one-time)
212	
213	1. Generate the updater key and add the two `TAURI_SIGNING_*` secrets — see
214	   [DESKTOP_AUTO_UPDATE.md](./DESKTOP_AUTO_UPDATE.md).
215	2. Put the public key into `tauri.conf.json` → `plugins.updater.pubkey` (replace
216	   `REPLACE_WITH_UPDATER_PUBLIC_KEY`) and commit it.
217	3. Configure the mobile secrets in the `testflight` GitHub Environment,
218	   including registered device UDIDs,
219	   Apple signing secrets, and Vercel project secrets.
220	4. Tag `desktop-v0.5.0` (or your next version) and push. Verify the desktop job produces
221	   a Release with `Type_*.dmg`, `*.app.tar.gz`, `*.app.tar.gz.sig`, and
222	   `latest.json`, and that an older install sees the update.
223	5. Tag `mobile-v0.2.0` (or your next mobile version) and push. Open
224	   `https://type-ota.vercel.app` in Safari on a registered device and install it.
225	
226	---
227	
228	## 6. What runs when, and what it costs
229	
230	| Workflow | Trigger | Runners | Builds the app? |
231	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
232	| `ci.yml` | push to `main`/`master`; every PR commit, any branch — **except** changes that touch only `**.md` / `docs/**` | ubuntu ×2 | No — typecheck + unit tests |
233	| `ffi-bindings-check.yml` | PRs touching `crates/type-ffi/**`, `packages/mobile-core/**`, `scripts/check-ffi-surface.mjs`; manual | ubuntu (PRs); **macOS only on manual dispatch** — its `codegen` job is gated on `github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'` | No — surface check + codegen |
234	| `release.yml` | push of a `desktop-v*` tag; manual | ubuntu + **macOS** | **Yes** — `.dmg` + updater artifacts |
235	| `mobile-adhoc.yml` | push of a `mobile-v*` tag; manual | ubuntu + **macOS** | Yes — ad-hoc `.ipa` → Vercel OTA site + artifact/release asset |
236	
237	Things that trigger **nothing**: pushing a branch that has no open PR, and
238	pushing a tag outside the `desktop-v*` / `mobile-v*` namespaces.
239	
240	**Cost: none.** `oogxdd/type` is a public repository, and GitHub Actions is free
241	on standard runners for public repos — including `macos-latest`. The macOS
242	multiplier and the included-minutes pool that most guidance warns about apply to
243	*private* repositories. Nothing here is a reason to avoid a run; what a run
244	actually costs is wall-clock time and a little noise.
245	
246	Documentation-only changes are skipped declaratively via `paths-ignore` in
247	`ci.yml`, so there is nothing to remember per commit. The filter skips a run
248	only when **every** changed path matches, so a commit mixing docs and code still
249	runs — it fails in the safe direction.
250	
251	`[skip ci]` (or `[ci skip]`, `[no ci]`, `[skip actions]`) in a commit message
252	still works as a manual override. Avoid it for code changes: an opt-out you have
253	to remember gets forgotten exactly when you're in a hurry, which is when CI is
254	worth most.
255	
256	> **The marker is matched as a plain substring, anywhere in the message —
257	> including the body, and including inside backticks or a quotation.** Writing
258	> *about* it ("replaced the skip-marker convention with `paths-ignore`") silently
259	> suppresses that commit's run. This bit us on the very commit that added
260	> `paths-ignore`. If you need to mention it in a message, break it up or say
261	> "skip marker". Actions → CI → Run workflow re-runs checks afterwards.
262	
263	### Why the release build is always cold
264	
265	`swatinem/rust-cache@v2` is in both workflows, but the release build still
266	compiles from scratch every time, for three independent reasons:
267	
268	1. **Different operating systems.** `ci.yml`'s `rust` job runs on
269	   `ubuntu-latest`; `release.yml` runs on `macos-latest`. Rust caches are
270	   per-platform, so CI produces nothing the release job could restore. This is
271	   the dominant reason.
272	2. **Cache scoping by ref.** A tag push runs on `refs/tags/desktop-v1.2.3`.
273	   Actions restores from the current ref's scope, falling back to the default
274	   branch — so `main → tag` can work, but a cache *saved* under one tag is
275	   invisible to the next tag. Tag-to-tag reuse never happens.
276	3. **Different profiles.** `cargo test --workspace --lib` builds `debug`;
277	   `tauri build` builds `release`. Even on matching platforms you would reuse
278	   the downloaded crates, not the compiled dependencies.
279	
280	### Should you fix it?
281	
282	Probably not. Warming it means adding a `macos-latest` job on `main` that does a
283	release-profile build with a shared `shared-key`, which the tag job then
284	restores. Since the runners are free here, the cost is complexity rather than
285	money — an extra job on every push to `main`, plus a cache Actions evicts after
286	7 days unused, so at a weekly release cadence the warm cache is often gone by
287	the time you need it.
288	
289	**Your fastest path is local.** The repo's `target/` on a dev Mac stays warm
290	(~12 GB), so `npm run desktop:release <version>` rebuilds incrementally in a
291	couple of minutes. CI is the fallback for when you're away from that machine.
292	
293	If you do want it warmed, the shape is:
294	
295	```yaml
296	# ci.yml — new job, main only
297	warm-desktop-cache:
298	  if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
299	  runs-on: macos-latest
300	  steps:
301	    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
302	    - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@1.97.1
303	    - uses: swatinem/rust-cache@v2
304	      with:
305	        shared-key: desktop-macos-release
306	    - run: cargo build --release --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml
307	
308	# release.yml — desktop job restores it, never saves (a tag-scoped
309	# save can't be read by anything later)
310	- uses: swatinem/rust-cache@v2
311	  with:
312	    shared-key: desktop-macos-release
313	    save-if: false
314	```
315	
316	### Choosing CI or local per release
317	
318	Both paths produce identical artifacts and both create the GitHub Release, so
319	the risk is doing it twice for the same tag. The `setup` job guards against
320	that: it checks whether the release already carries a `latest.json`, and the
321	whole `desktop` job is skipped if so. The check deliberately lives in `setup`
322	rather than inside the macOS job, so a local release wastes seconds of CI
323	rather than spinning up a macOS runner to do nothing. That makes the choice a
324	matter of what you do first, with no flags to remember:
325	
326	- **Local:** `npm run desktop:release 1.2.3`. It builds, signs, publishes, and
327	  creates the tag. If that tag push wakes CI, CI sees the finished release and
328	  skips.
329	- **CI:** just push the tag — `git tag desktop-v1.2.3 && git push origin
330	  desktop-v1.2.3`. Nothing is published yet, so CI builds it.
331	
332	### Local release credentials — use the Keychain, not a dotenv
333	
334	`release-local.sh` resolves everything it needs by itself, so a local release is
335	one command with no exports. It looks in this order: existing environment →
336	login Keychain → derived from the machine.
337	
338	Derived for free: the updater private key from `~/.tauri/type-updater.key`, the
339	signing identity from `security find-identity`, and the Team ID from that
340	identity's `(TEAMID)` suffix.
341	
342	The three actual secrets go in the Keychain once:
343	
344	```bash
345	security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s type-updater-key-password -w
346	security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s type-apple-app-password -w
347	security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s type-apple-id -w
348	```
349	
350	`-w` with no value prompts for it, so nothing lands in shell history.
351	
352	**Why not a `.env` file:** these are release-signing secrets. A dotenv is
353	plaintext on disk and one `.gitignore` slip from being committed, and it invites
354	copies to spread. Keychain items are encrypted at rest, survive across shells,
355	and live where the Developer ID certificate already is. Plain `export` in a
356	shell is worse still — it lasts only until you close the window, and typing the
357	password inline puts it in history.
358	
359	Environment variables still win when set, so CI and one-off overrides keep
360	working unchanged.
361	
362	If the Apple credentials are missing, the script warns and builds **unsigned**
363	rather than failing. Take that warning seriously: shipping an unsigned update to
364	people running a notarized build means macOS refuses to launch their next fresh
365	install.
366	
367	---
368	
369	## 7. Later: dedicated macOS runners (e.g. getmac.io / self-hosted)
370	
371	Out of scope for now — high-level only. When free minutes stop being enough and
372	local builds get tedious, point the macOS job at a faster/cheaper runner:
373	
374	- **Self-hosted / third-party macOS runner** (getmac.io, MacStadium, a Mac mini):
375	  register it as a GitHub self-hosted runner with a label like `macos-getmac`,
376	  then change `runs-on: macos-latest` → `runs-on: [self-hosted, macOS, macos-getmac]`
377	  in the `desktop` job. Everything else (steps, secrets) stays the same.
378	- Pre-install Node, Rust, and Xcode on the runner image so jobs skip toolchain
379	  setup; keep `swatinem/rust-cache` for incremental Rust builds.
380	- Persisted signing material can live in the runner's Keychain instead of
381	  importing certs each run — or keep using the secrets for reproducibility.
382

# Releasing — versioning & CI

Desktop (macOS Tauri app, auto-updates in-app) and mobile (React Native /
Expo) releases are **tag-driven** and intentionally separate.

- The **git tag is the release trigger and the source of truth for the version.**
  You don't have to commit a version bump — tagging *is* the release. CI reads the
  version out of the tag and writes it into the app config before building. (The
  version committed in the repo is just the dev baseline.)
- See also: [DESKTOP_AUTO_UPDATE.md](./DESKTOP_AUTO_UPDATE.md) for the desktop
  updater internals, and [UPDATER_KEY_ROTATION.md](./UPDATER_KEY_ROTATION.md)
  for generating or rotating the signing key.
- For future Mac App Store / TestFlight releases, see
  [MACOS_APP_STORE_TESTFLIGHT.md](./MACOS_APP_STORE_TESTFLIGHT.md).

---

## 1. Versioning model

**Separate tag namespaces.** Desktop and mobile can move independently:

```
desktop-v0.5.0   desktop 0.5.0
mobile-v0.2.0    mobile 0.2.0
desktop-v0.5.1   desktop 0.5.1
```

> Why GitHub's *latest* release matters for the updater: the desktop updater
> reads `…/releases/latest/download/latest.json`, so the desktop release must be
> marked as GitHub's latest release. The desktop workflow forces the `latest`
> flag on every desktop release. Mobile releases are also listed on GitHub,
> but are explicitly prevented from replacing the latest desktop release.

---

## 2. How to cut a desktop release

### Option A — push a tag (normal path)

```bash
git checkout main && git pull          # release from main
npm version 0.5.0 --no-git-tag-version  # optional: keep repo baseline in sync
git commit -am "Release 0.5.0" || true

git tag desktop-v0.5.0
git push origin desktop-v0.5.0
```

CI ([`.github/workflows/release.yml`](../.github/workflows/release.yml)) builds
the `.dmg` + updater artifacts and publishes the GitHub Release.

### Option B — manual run (no tag)

Actions tab → **Desktop Release** → **Run workflow** → enter the version.
Useful for re-running a failed build.

### Option C — build locally

CI is not rationed here: `oogxdd/type` is public, and GitHub Actions is free on
standard runners for public repositories. Build locally for *speed*, not cost —
a cold CI build takes 8–10 minutes, while your Mac rebuilds incrementally in
about two:

```bash
# desktop needs the updater signing key in the environment:
export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY="$(cat ~/.tauri/type-updater.key)"
export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD="<password>"

apps/desktop/scripts/release-local.sh 0.5.0
```

It bumps the version, builds, signs, assembles `latest.json`, and creates the
GitHub Release via `gh` — exactly what CI does. (`gh auth login` required once.)

---

## 2b. Developing locally without touching the installed prod app

The released app and a local dev build are **fully separate installs with
separate data**, as long as you use the dev config. Never point a dev run at the
production identifier — `com.digital.type2`'s app-data directory is where the
real notes live.

| | Production | Dev |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bundle | `/Applications/Type.app` | `/Applications/Type Dev.app` |
| Identifier | `com.digital.type2` | `com.digital.type2.dev` |
| App data (notes, profiles, keys) | `~/Library/Application Support/com.digital.type2` | `~/Library/Application Support/com.digital.type2.dev` |
| Auto-update | on (GitHub `latest.json`) | off (`endpoints: []`) |

Everything above the identifier line is driven by
`apps/desktop/src-tauri/tauri.dev.conf.json`, which Tauri deep-merges over
`tauri.conf.json`.

```bash
npm run desktop:app       # dev run against the dev identifier — safe
npm run desktop:dmg:dev   # "Type Dev.dmg", installs alongside prod
```

`npm run desktop:app:prod-data` exists as an explicit escape hatch: it runs the
dev build against the **production** app-data directory. Use it only when you
deliberately need to reproduce something against real notes, and back up first
(see below).

The dev config sets `plugins.updater.endpoints: []`, so a dev build can never
download and overwrite itself with a production release. The updater errors with
`EmptyEndpoints` if you press "Check for updates" there — that is intended.

### Backing up production data

Everything the desktop app owns lives under one directory:

```bash
STAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
rsync -aH --exclude 'whisper/' --exclude '.DS_Store' \
  "$HOME/Library/Application Support/com.digital.type2/" \
  "/Volumes/KINGSTON/Backups/type/prod-$STAMP/app-data/"
ditto /Applications/Type.app "/Volumes/KINGSTON/Backups/type/prod-$STAMP/Type.app"
```

`whisper/` is excluded because the managed Python env re-provisions itself.
Everything that matters — `notes/`, `profiles/`, `config.json`,
`.notes-profiles.json`, `local_sync/` — is a few tens of MB.

---

## 3. How to cut a mobile release

For the native Xcode ad-hoc build, signing, and OTA deployment used by the
GitHub-hosted macOS runner, see
[MOBILE_AD_HOC_GITHUB_ACTIONS.md](./MOBILE_AD_HOC_GITHUB_ACTIONS.md).

```bash
git checkout main && git pull
git tag mobile-v0.2.0
git push origin mobile-v0.2.0
```

CI ([`.github/workflows/mobile-adhoc.yml`](../.github/workflows/mobile-adhoc.yml)):

1. creates a GitHub Release without changing the desktop Latest,
2. runs on a macOS runner,
3. generates the iOS UniFFI/native module from `packages/mobile-core`,
4. archives and exports an ad-hoc `.ipa` with Xcode,
5. verifies its signature, version, and registered-device profile,
6. uploads it as a workflow artifact and tagged GitHub Release asset, and
7. deploys the OTA install site to `https://type-ota.vercel.app`.

The workflow sets `MOBILE_VERSION` from the tag and uses the GitHub run number
as `IOS_BUILD_NUMBER`. For a manual run, use Actions → **Mobile Ad Hoc** and
optionally enter an explicit build number. Manual dispatch updates the OTA site
and keeps the IPA as a 30-day workflow artifact but does not create a GitHub
Release; the `github-release` job runs only for a pushed `mobile-v*` tag.

---

## 4. Required GitHub secrets

Add under **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions**.

### Mobile (required)

The `ios` job keeps using the existing `testflight` GitHub Environment so its
Apple API-key secrets remain available; the legacy environment name does not
mean the workflow uploads to TestFlight. Add the following as environment
secrets (or repository secrets if environment scoping is not desired):

| Secret | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `APPLE_TEAM_ID` | Apple Developer team ID |
| `APP_STORE_CONNECT_KEY_ID` | Team App Store Connect API key ID |
| `APP_STORE_CONNECT_ISSUER_ID` | Team App Store Connect API issuer ID |
| `APP_STORE_CONNECT_PRIVATE_KEY` | Complete contents of the API key `.p8` file |
| `IOS_DISTRIBUTION_CERTIFICATE_BASE64` | Base64-encoded Apple Distribution `.p12` including its private key |
| `IOS_DISTRIBUTION_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | Password for that `.p12` |
| `IOS_AD_HOC_DEVICE_UDIDS` | Required registered device UDIDs, separated by commas, spaces, or newlines |
| `VERCEL_TOKEN` | Token with deploy access to the OTA project |

`IOS_AD_HOC_BASE_URL`, `VERCEL_ORG_ID`, and `VERCEL_PROJECT_ID` are optional
repository variables. The workflow defaults them to the existing production
URL and Vercel project.

The runner imports the distribution identity into a temporary Keychain; Xcode
uses the API key for automatic provisioning and exports with
`ExportOptionsAdHoc.plist`. Expo/EAS and TestFlight are not used. See
[MOBILE_AD_HOC_GITHUB_ACTIONS.md](./MOBILE_AD_HOC_GITHUB_ACTIONS.md) for setup.

### Desktop (required)

| Secret                                | What it is                                            |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY`           | Contents of `~/.tauri/type-updater.key`               |
| `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD`  | Password for that key                                 |

`GITHUB_TOKEN` is provided automatically (used to create the Release).

### Desktop — Apple notarization (optional)

Without these the `.dmg` still works but triggers the "unidentified developer"
warning on first open. With them, tauri-action notarizes automatically:
`APPLE_CERTIFICATE`, `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD`, `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY`,
`APPLE_ID`, `APPLE_PASSWORD`, `APPLE_TEAM_ID`.

Set **all six or none** — a partially configured setup fails the release rather
than falling back to unsigned. Full walkthrough, including the microphone
entitlement the hardened runtime requires:
[MACOS_CODE_SIGNING.md](./MACOS_CODE_SIGNING.md).

---

## 5. First-release checklist (one-time)

1. Generate the updater key and add the two `TAURI_SIGNING_*` secrets — see
   [DESKTOP_AUTO_UPDATE.md](./DESKTOP_AUTO_UPDATE.md).
2. Put the public key into `tauri.conf.json` → `plugins.updater.pubkey` (replace
   `REPLACE_WITH_UPDATER_PUBLIC_KEY`) and commit it.
3. Configure the mobile secrets in the `testflight` GitHub Environment,
   including registered device UDIDs,
   Apple signing secrets, and Vercel project secrets.
4. Tag `desktop-v0.5.0` (or your next version) and push. Verify the desktop job produces
   a Release with `Type_*.dmg`, `*.app.tar.gz`, `*.app.tar.gz.sig`, and
   `latest.json`, and that an older install sees the update.
5. Tag `mobile-v0.2.0` (or your next mobile version) and push. Open
   `https://type-ota.vercel.app` in Safari on a registered device and install it.

---

## 6. What runs when, and what it costs

| Workflow | Trigger | Runners | Builds the app? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ci.yml` | push to `main`/`master`; every PR commit, any branch — **except** changes that touch only `**.md` / `docs/**` | ubuntu ×2 | No — typecheck + unit tests |
| `ffi-bindings-check.yml` | PRs touching `crates/type-ffi/**`, `packages/mobile-core/**`, `scripts/check-ffi-surface.mjs`; manual | ubuntu (PRs); **macOS only on manual dispatch** — its `codegen` job is gated on `github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'` | No — surface check + codegen |
| `release.yml` | push of a `desktop-v*` tag; manual | ubuntu + **macOS** | **Yes** — `.dmg` + updater artifacts |
| `mobile-adhoc.yml` | push of a `mobile-v*` tag; manual | ubuntu + **macOS** | Yes — ad-hoc `.ipa` → Vercel OTA site + artifact/release asset |

Things that trigger **nothing**: pushing a branch that has no open PR, and
pushing a tag outside the `desktop-v*` / `mobile-v*` namespaces.

**Cost: none.** `oogxdd/type` is a public repository, and GitHub Actions is free
on standard runners for public repos — including `macos-latest`. The macOS
multiplier and the included-minutes pool that most guidance warns about apply to
*private* repositories. Nothing here is a reason to avoid a run; what a run
actually costs is wall-clock time and a little noise.

Documentation-only changes are skipped declaratively via `paths-ignore` in
`ci.yml`, so there is nothing to remember per commit. The filter skips a run
only when **every** changed path matches, so a commit mixing docs and code still
runs — it fails in the safe direction.

`[skip ci]` (or `[ci skip]`, `[no ci]`, `[skip actions]`) in a commit message
still works as a manual override. Avoid it for code changes: an opt-out you have
to remember gets forgotten exactly when you're in a hurry, which is when CI is
worth most.

> **The marker is matched as a plain substring, anywhere in the message —
> including the body, and including inside backticks or a quotation.** Writing
> *about* it ("replaced the skip-marker convention with `paths-ignore`") silently
> suppresses that commit's run. This bit us on the very commit that added
> `paths-ignore`. If you need to mention it in a message, break it up or say
> "skip marker". Actions → CI → Run workflow re-runs checks afterwards.

### Why the release build is always cold

`swatinem/rust-cache@v2` is in both workflows, but the release build still
compiles from scratch every time, for three independent reasons:

1. **Different operating systems.** `ci.yml`'s `rust` job runs on
   `ubuntu-latest`; `release.yml` runs on `macos-latest`. Rust caches are
   per-platform, so CI produces nothing the release job could restore. This is
   the dominant reason.
2. **Cache scoping by ref.** A tag push runs on `refs/tags/desktop-v1.2.3`.
   Actions restores from the current ref's scope, falling back to the default
   branch — so `main → tag` can work, but a cache *saved* under one tag is
   invisible to the next tag. Tag-to-tag reuse never happens.
3. **Different profiles.** `cargo test --workspace --lib` builds `debug`;
   `tauri build` builds `release`. Even on matching platforms you would reuse
   the downloaded crates, not the compiled dependencies.

### Should you fix it?

Probably not. Warming it means adding a `macos-latest` job on `main` that does a
release-profile build with a shared `shared-key`, which the tag job then
restores. Since the runners are free here, the cost is complexity rather than
money — an extra job on every push to `main`, plus a cache Actions evicts after
7 days unused, so at a weekly release cadence the warm cache is often gone by
the time you need it.

**Your fastest path is local.** The repo's `target/` on a dev Mac stays warm
(~12 GB), so `npm run desktop:release <version>` rebuilds incrementally in a
couple of minutes. CI is the fallback for when you're away from that machine.

If you do want it warmed, the shape is:

```yaml
# ci.yml — new job, main only
warm-desktop-cache:
  if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
  runs-on: macos-latest
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@1.97.1
    - uses: swatinem/rust-cache@v2
      with:
        shared-key: desktop-macos-release
    - run: cargo build --release --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml

# release.yml — desktop job restores it, never saves (a tag-scoped
# save can't be read by anything later)
- uses: swatinem/rust-cache@v2
  with:
    shared-key: desktop-macos-release
    save-if: false
```

### Choosing CI or local per release

Both paths produce identical artifacts and both create the GitHub Release, so
the risk is doing it twice for the same tag. The `setup` job guards against
that: it checks whether the release already carries a `latest.json`, and the
whole `desktop` job is skipped if so. The check deliberately lives in `setup`
rather than inside the macOS job, so a local release wastes seconds of CI
rather than spinning up a macOS runner to do nothing. That makes the choice a
matter of what you do first, with no flags to remember:

- **Local:** `npm run desktop:release 1.2.3`. It builds, signs, publishes, and
  creates the tag. If that tag push wakes CI, CI sees the finished release and
  skips.
- **CI:** just push the tag — `git tag desktop-v1.2.3 && git push origin
  desktop-v1.2.3`. Nothing is published yet, so CI builds it.

### Local release credentials — use the Keychain, not a dotenv

`release-local.sh` resolves everything it needs by itself, so a local release is
one command with no exports. It looks in this order: existing environment →
login Keychain → derived from the machine.

Derived for free: the updater private key from `~/.tauri/type-updater.key`, the
signing identity from `security find-identity`, and the Team ID from that
identity's `(TEAMID)` suffix.

The three actual secrets go in the Keychain once:

```bash
security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s type-updater-key-password -w
security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s type-apple-app-password -w
security add-generic-password -a "$USER" -s type-apple-id -w
```

`-w` with no value prompts for it, so nothing lands in shell history.

**Why not a `.env` file:** these are release-signing secrets. A dotenv is
plaintext on disk and one `.gitignore` slip from being committed, and it invites
copies to spread. Keychain items are encrypted at rest, survive across shells,
and live where the Developer ID certificate already is. Plain `export` in a
shell is worse still — it lasts only until you close the window, and typing the
password inline puts it in history.

Environment variables still win when set, so CI and one-off overrides keep
working unchanged.

If the Apple credentials are missing, the script warns and builds **unsigned**
rather than failing. Take that warning seriously: shipping an unsigned update to
people running a notarized build means macOS refuses to launch their next fresh
install.

---

## 7. Later: dedicated macOS runners (e.g. getmac.io / self-hosted)

Out of scope for now — high-level only. When free minutes stop being enough and
local builds get tedious, point the macOS job at a faster/cheaper runner:

- **Self-hosted / third-party macOS runner** (getmac.io, MacStadium, a Mac mini):
  register it as a GitHub self-hosted runner with a label like `macos-getmac`,
  then change `runs-on: macos-latest` → `runs-on: [self-hosted, macOS, macos-getmac]`
  in the `desktop` job. Everything else (steps, secrets) stays the same.
- Pre-install Node, Rust, and Xcode on the runner image so jobs skip toolchain
  setup; keep `swatinem/rust-cache` for incremental Rust builds.
- Persisted signing material can live in the runner's Keychain instead of
  importing certs each run — or keep using the secrets for reproducibility.

Locally there's a huge pile (~40 `entire/*` session-checkpoint branches, several `codex/*` experiments, a few `archive/*`, and worktree branches) — most are dead weight, not real pending work. The ones that actually look like live, unmerged feature work:

- `feat/object-storage-sync`, `feat/sync-request-window`, `feature/icloud-folder-sync`, `fix/ios-codegen-deployment-target`, `docs/sync-ios-release-guides`, `desktop-state-rehaul`, `agent/document-ios-testflight-actions` (local+remote)
- Remote-only: `origin/agent/iroh-docs-filesystem-sync`, `origin/agent/iroh-encrypted-sync-peer`, `origin/worktree-mobile-assemblyai`, `origin/worktree-mobile-audio-transcription`

None of these are merged into `main`, but none look required for a release either — they read as in-progress experiments. Say the word if you want me to check any specific one before we ship.

## 2) What changed since the last releases

**Desktop** (last tag `desktop-v0.5.0`, 2026‑09‑05) — 11 commits: persistent colored tags + a synced `.type/tags.json` registry, a unified review pane for selected notes, the new notes MCP (skip-ai filtering, scoped agent workspace), command-palette additions (note splitting, untitled rename), a Cmd+K/shortcut cleanup ("every shortcut has one owner"), unified desktop nav trees, and deleting a note's recording/attachment along with the note.

**Mobile** (last tag `mobile-v0.2.7`, 2026‑09‑02) — a lot more, and notably **several version bumps (0.2.8 → 0.2.13) were committed but never tagged/shipped**. Highlights: capture-swipe crash fixes (SIGABRT recursion, native-back-gesture zoning), swipe-up made easier, custom mobile colors/fonts, a Diagnostics toggle for sync status, menu quick-sync, Iroh audio-archive hang fix + notes-then-audio sync split, and the mobile release pipeline itself was swapped from TestFlight to ad-hoc distribution.

## 3) Can I cut a release?

**Desktop: yes.** All required CI secrets exist (`TAURI_SIGNING_*`, Apple notarization x6), the last 5 tag-triggered `Desktop Release` runs succeeded, and `main`'s CI is currently green. Cutting `desktop-v0.5.1` (or whatever version) by pushing a tag should just work. Local build is also possible via `apps/desktop/scripts/release-local.sh`, but the Keychain items it needs (updater key password, Apple ID/app-password) aren't set up on this machine — you'd add those yourself.

**Mobile: blocked.** The `Mobile Ad Hoc` workflow (which builds the ad-hoc `.ipa` and deploys the OTA site you'd install from on your iPhone) needs 4 secrets in the `testflight` GitHub environment that are **missing**: `IOS_DISTRIBUTION_CERTIFICATE_BASE64`, `IOS_DISTRIBUTION_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD`, `IOS_AD_HOC_DEVICE_UDIDS`, `VERCEL_TOKEN`. (The App Store Connect API key secrets are already there.) These are real Apple/Vercel credentials — I won't generate or handle them, you'd add them yourself, e.g.:

```
gh secret set IOS_DISTRIBUTION_CERTIFICATE_BASE64 --env testflight < cert-base64.txt
gh secret set IOS_DISTRIBUTION_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD --env testflight
gh secret set IOS_AD_HOC_DEVICE_UDIDS --env testflight
gh secret set VERCEL_TOKEN --env testflight
```
Full instructions (getting the `.p12`, finding your UDID, Vercel token scope) are in `docs/MOBILE_AD_HOC_GITHUB_ACTIONS.md`. Once those are set, `git tag mobile-v0.2.13 && git push origin mobile-v0.2.13` would produce an install link at `type-ota.vercel.app`.

content.content:
1	# Ad-hoc: building and installing the iOS app without TestFlight
2	
3	Ad-hoc is the normal mobile release route. Push a `mobile-v*` tag and
4	`.github/workflows/mobile-adhoc.yml` builds a signed `.ipa`, verifies that the
5	configured devices are in its provisioning profile, stores it as a workflow
6	artifact and GitHub Release asset, and deploys the install page to
7	`https://type-ota.vercel.app`.
8	
9	The local build instructions below remain as a fallback and as a way to debug
10	signing. CI and local builds use the same native-code generation, Xcode archive,
11	`ExportOptionsAdHoc.plist`, and OTA generator.
12	
13	> **Read this before installing.** An ad-hoc build carries a different signature
14	> than the TestFlight copy of the same bundle id, so iOS refuses to install one
15	> over the other. The existing app must be deleted first, and **that erases its
16	> container — notes, sync settings, and the device's SSH key.** Sync from the
17	> phone first. If the same version is already on TestFlight, install it from
18	> there instead: that path updates in place and keeps the data.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## GitHub Actions release (normal route)
23	
24	The one-time setup, secrets, and release flow are documented in
25	[`docs/MOBILE_AD_HOC_GITHUB_ACTIONS.md`](../../docs/MOBILE_AD_HOC_GITHUB_ACTIONS.md).
26	For a release from `main`:
27	
28	```sh
29	git tag mobile-v0.2.7
30	git push origin mobile-v0.2.7
31	```
32	
33	When the **Mobile Ad Hoc** workflow succeeds, open
34	`https://type-ota.vercel.app` in Safari on a registered device. A manual run is
35	also available under Actions and accepts an explicit version/build number.
36	
37	## Local-build prerequisites
38	
39	- Apple Developer Program membership, team `Y377P5XKGJ`.
40	- App Store Connect API key at
41	  `~/.appstoreconnect/private_keys/AuthKey_W2Y52J5N33.p8`
42	  (issuer `bd0c62da-fcbf-4770-a10d-2ee30da0963e`). Same key CI uses.
43	  **No local Apple Distribution certificate or `.p12` is needed** — `security
44	  find-identity -v -p codesigning` on this Mac normally shows only an "Apple
45	  Development" identity, never "Apple Distribution". That is fine: §1.5's
46	  archive step only needs *some* valid identity (Development is enough), and
47	  §1.6's `-exportArchive -allowProvisioningUpdates` is what actually gets the
48	  Distribution certificate — the API key lets Xcode fetch/provision it from
49	  App Store Connect during export, without ever touching the local keychain.
50	  Don't go hunting for a `.p12` or let Xcode create a certificate by hand
51	  first; just run the documented archive + export commands and let export
52	  handle it. (Verified 2026-09-04: archived with "Apple Development", the
53	  exported `.ipa` came back signed "Apple Distribution: Maxim Ignatev
54	  (Y377P5XKGJ)", and `security find-identity` was unchanged before and after —
55	  no certificate was created or consumed locally.)
56	- **The target device's UDID registered in the developer account.** Ad-hoc
57	  provisioning profiles embed a device list; export fails while building the
58	  profile if the device is not on it. Get the UDID from Xcode → Window → Devices
59	  and Simulators (the "Identifier" field), or `xcrun devicectl list devices`,
60	  and register it at developer.apple.com → Devices.
61	- Xcode with the iOS SDK, CocoaPods, and a Rust toolchain with the
62	  `aarch64-apple-ios` target.
63	- For the Vercel path: `vercel` CLI, logged in (`vercel whoami`).
64	
65	Run everything from the repo root unless a step says otherwise.
66	
67	---
68	
69	## 1. Build the .ipa
70	
71	### 1.1 Checks
72	
73	```sh
74	npm run typecheck -w @typenotes/mobile
75	npm run test -w @typenotes/mobile
76	```
77	
78	### 1.2 Set the version
79	
80	`apps/mobile/app.config.js` reads `MOBILE_VERSION` and `IOS_BUILD_NUMBER` from
81	the environment and overrides whatever `app.json` says — that is how CI gets the
82	version from the tag without a commit. `expo prebuild` bakes those values into
83	`apps/mobile/ios/Type/Info.plist` as **literals**, not as `$(MARKETING_VERSION)`
84	references.
85	
86	That last detail is the trap: passing `MARKETING_VERSION=` /
87	`CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION=` on the `xcodebuild` command line does nothing,
88	because `Info.plist` no longer refers to those build settings. An archive built
89	that way silently carries the old version.
90	
91	So either re-run prebuild with the environment set:
92	
93	```sh
94	cd apps/mobile
95	MOBILE_VERSION=0.2.6 IOS_BUILD_NUMBER=2026090101 npx expo prebuild --platform ios
96	```
97	
98	…or edit the two files by hand and keep them in sync:
99	
100	- `apps/mobile/app.json` — `expo.version`, `expo.ios.buildNumber`
101	- `apps/mobile/ios/Type/Info.plist` — `CFBundleShortVersionString`,
102	  `CFBundleVersion`
103	
104	`apps/mobile/ios/` is tracked, so inspect the diff after a prebuild. Only use
105	`--clean` after changing Expo config, plugins, or native dependencies.
106	
107	### 1.3 Regenerate the Rust core with a device slice
108	
109	The checked-in `packages/mobile-core/src/index.tsx` is a mock fallback so clean
110	clones and Expo Go work. A device build needs the real UniFFI turbo module:
111	
112	```sh
113	IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=16.4 npm run codegen:ios:device -w @typenotes/mobile-core
114	```
115	
116	`codegen:ios` (no `:device`) builds a **simulator-only** slice — it will archive
117	and then fail to link or run on hardware. Verify the package did not stay in
118	demo mode:
119	
120	```sh
121	test -f packages/mobile-core/TypeCore.podspec
122	test -f packages/mobile-core/TypenotesMobileCoreFramework.xcframework/ios-arm64/libtype_ffi.a
123	grep -q 'Generated by uniffi-bindgen-react-native' packages/mobile-core/src/index.tsx
124	! grep -q '__isDemoCore' packages/mobile-core/src/index.tsx
125	```
126	
127	Codegen overwrites `src/index.tsx`, so `git status` will show it modified
128	afterwards. That is expected — **do not commit it**; restore the fallback with
129	`git checkout -- packages/mobile-core/src/index.tsx` when done. The file cannot
130	be gitignored: `package.json` declares it as the package `main`, so a clean
131	clone without it has no entry point at all.
132	
133	### 1.4 Pods
134	
135	```sh
136	cd apps/mobile/ios
137	pod install
138	```
139	
140	Run it from that directory. `pod install --project-directory=apps/mobile/ios`
141	from the repo root fails — the `Podfile` resolves React Native's location from
142	`Dir.pwd`, so it looks for `apps/mobile/node_modules/react-native` and does not
143	find the hoisted copy.
144	
145	Confirm `Pods/Target Support Files/Pods-Type/Pods-Type.release.xcconfig`
146	contains `-lz -liconv`; the `Podfile` post-install hook adds them, and they are
147	required because `libtype_ffi.a` statically includes libgit2.
148	
149	### 1.5 Archive
150	
151	From `apps/mobile/ios`:
152	
153	```sh
154	xcodebuild -workspace Type.xcworkspace -scheme Type -configuration Release \
155	  -destination "generic/platform=iOS" -archivePath build/Type.xcarchive archive \
156	  DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=Y377P5XKGJ CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Automatic -allowProvisioningUpdates \
157	  -authenticationKeyPath ~/.appstoreconnect/private_keys/AuthKey_W2Y52J5N33.p8 \
158	  -authenticationKeyID W2Y52J5N33 \
159	  -authenticationKeyIssuerID bd0c62da-fcbf-4770-a10d-2ee30da0963e
160	```
161	
162	Check the version before spending an export on it:
163	
164	```sh
165	/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy \
166	  -c "Print :ApplicationProperties:CFBundleShortVersionString" \
167	  -c "Print :ApplicationProperties:CFBundleVersion" \
168	  build/Type.xcarchive/Info.plist
169	```
170	
171	### 1.6 Export ad-hoc
172	
173	`ExportOptionsAdHoc.plist` is the ad-hoc counterpart to `ExportOptions.plist`
174	(App Store). `release-testing` is Xcode 15+'s name for the method previously
175	called `ad-hoc`.
176	
177	```sh
178	xcodebuild -exportArchive -archivePath build/Type.xcarchive \
179	  -exportOptionsPlist ../ExportOptionsAdHoc.plist \
180	  -exportPath build/export-adhoc \
181	  -allowProvisioningUpdates \
182	  -authenticationKeyPath ~/.appstoreconnect/private_keys/AuthKey_W2Y52J5N33.p8 \
183	  -authenticationKeyID W2Y52J5N33 \
184	  -authenticationKeyIssuerID bd0c62da-fcbf-4770-a10d-2ee30da0963e
185	```
186	
187	### 1.7 Verify the .ipa
188	
189	Confirm both the version and that the target device made it into the embedded
190	profile — a profile missing the device produces an "unable to install" that
191	looks identical to a signing failure:
192	
193	```sh
194	cd $(mktemp -d) && unzip -q /path/to/build/export-adhoc/Type.ipa
195	
196	/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy \
197	  -c "Print :CFBundleShortVersionString" \
198	  -c "Print :CFBundleVersion" \
199	  -c "Print :CFBundleIdentifier" \
200	  Payload/Type.app/Info.plist
201	
202	security cms -D -i Payload/Type.app/embedded.mobileprovision > prof.plist
203	/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy -c "Print :Name" -c "Print :ProvisionedDevices" prof.plist
204	```
205	
206	Expect `iOS Team Ad Hoc Provisioning Profile: com.typenotes.mobile` and the
207	device's UDID in the list.
208	
209	---
210	
211	## 2. Distribute over the air
212	
213	iOS installs a signed build from a plain web page: Safari opens an
214	`itms-services://` URL, that fetches a manifest, and the manifest points at the
215	`.ipa`. Both files must come over **HTTPS with a publicly trusted certificate**
216	— true since iOS 7.1; a self-signed certificate is rejected unless its CA is
217	installed and explicitly trusted on the device.
218	
219	This changes delivery only. The build is still ad-hoc signed, so only devices in
220	the profile can install it.
221	
222	### 2.1 Generate the site
223	
224	`scripts/ota.mjs` reads the bundle id, version, and build number out of the
225	`.ipa` itself rather than from `app.json`, because iOS matches the manifest
226	against the payload and a `bundle-version` that disagrees makes the install
227	silently do nothing.
228	
229	```sh
230	npm run ota -w @typenotes/mobile -- build \
231	  ios/build/export-adhoc/Type.ipa \
232	  --base-url https://type-ota.vercel.app
233	```
234	
235	Writes `apps/mobile/ios/build/ota/` (override with `--out`):
236	
237	| file | |
238	|---|---|
239	| `index.html` | landing page with the Install button |
240	| `manifest.plist` | what `itms-services` fetches |
241	| `Type.ipa` | the payload |
242	| `vercel.json` | content types — hosts otherwise guess wrong for `.plist` |
243	
244	### 2.2 Deploy to Vercel
245	
246	The manifest needs **absolute** URLs, so the host URL has to be known before
247	generating. First time round it is not, so deploy twice:
248	
249	```sh
250	cd apps/mobile/ios/build/ota
251	vercel deploy --prod --yes                       # 1. learn the URL
252	vercel inspect <deployment-url> | grep -A3 Aliases
253	```
254	
255	Take the stable alias — for this project, `https://type-ota.vercel.app` — then
256	regenerate with it and redeploy:
257	
258	```sh
259	npm run ota -w @typenotes/mobile -- build \
260	  ios/build/export-adhoc/Type.ipa --base-url https://type-ota.vercel.app
261	cd apps/mobile/ios/build/ota && vercel deploy --prod --yes
262	```
263	
264	Vercel content-addresses uploads, so the second push of the same 30 MB payload
265	is near-instant. **Later releases are a single pass** — the alias is stable, so
266	generate with `--base-url https://type-ota.vercel.app` and deploy once.
267	
268	The Vercel project name comes from the directory name (`ota` → adjust with
269	`vercel link` if you want something else). The existing project is `type-ota`
270	under `maxim-ignatevs-projects-ef3992aa`.
271	
272	### 2.3 Verify before touching the phone
273	
274	```sh
275	curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "index: %{http_code} %{content_type}\n"    https://type-ota.vercel.app/
276	curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "manifest: %{http_code} %{content_type}\n" https://type-ota.vercel.app/manifest.plist
277	curl -sSI https://type-ota.vercel.app/Type.ipa | grep -iE "^HTTP|content-type|content-length"
278	```
279	
280	Expect `text/html`, `text/xml`, and `application/octet-stream`. A `401` means
281	Vercel Deployment Protection is on for the project — turn it off in the
282	project's settings, or the phone gets a login wall instead of the app.
283	
284	Also confirm the manifest picked up the right URL and version:
285	
286	```sh
287	curl -sS https://type-ota.vercel.app/manifest.plist | grep '<string>'
288	```
289	
290	### 2.4 Install
291	
292	Open `https://type-ota.vercel.app` **in Safari on the device** and tap Install.
293	Other browsers ignore the `itms-services` scheme and the button does nothing.
294	The icon appears on the home screen with a progress ring; the first launch may
295	need Settings → General → VPN & Device Management to trust the developer.
296	
297	The URL is public — anyone can download the binary, though only registered
298	devices can install it. Delete the Vercel project when done if that matters.
299	
300	---
301	
302	## 3. Alternative: local server behind a tunnel
303	
304	For a one-off install with nothing left hosted anywhere:
305	
306	```sh
307	npm run ota -w @typenotes/mobile -- serve ios/build/export-adhoc/Type.ipa
308	# in another shell:
309	cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8787     # or: ngrok http 8787
310	```
311	
312	Open the tunnel's HTTPS URL in Safari. The server generates the manifest per
313	request from the `Host` / `X-Forwarded-Proto` headers, so the public URL does
314	not have to be known in advance and nothing needs regenerating when the tunnel
315	comes up with a fresh address. Neither tunnel client is installed by default
316	(`brew install cloudflared`).
317	
318	## 4. Alternative: cable
319	
320	Xcode → Window → Devices and Simulators → select the device → drag the `.ipa`
321	into "Installed Apps", or use Apple Configurator. No HTTPS, no hosting; the
322	device has to be connected and unlocked. Note that AirDropping an `.ipa` or
323	opening it from Files does **not** work — iOS will not install it that way.
324	
325	---
326	
327	## Troubleshooting
328	
329	| symptom | cause |
330	|---|---|
331	| Export fails building the provisioning profile | device UDID not registered in the account |
332	| Install button does nothing | page opened in a browser other than Safari |
333	| "Unable to install" | device not in the embedded profile (§1.7), or a differently-signed copy of the same bundle id is already installed |
334	| Install starts, then the icon greys out permanently | manifest `bundle-identifier` / `bundle-version` disagree with the payload |
335	| Safari shows the manifest as text | host served `.plist` with the wrong content type — `vercel.json` fixes this on Vercel |
336	| Phone gets a Vercel login page | Deployment Protection enabled on the project |

# Ad-hoc: building and installing the iOS app without TestFlight

Ad-hoc is the normal mobile release route. Push a `mobile-v*` tag and
`.github/workflows/mobile-adhoc.yml` builds a signed `.ipa`, verifies that the
configured devices are in its provisioning profile, stores it as a workflow
artifact and GitHub Release asset, and deploys the install page to
`https://type-ota.vercel.app`.

The local build instructions below remain as a fallback and as a way to debug
signing. CI and local builds use the same native-code generation, Xcode archive,
`ExportOptionsAdHoc.plist`, and OTA generator.

> **Read this before installing.** An ad-hoc build carries a different signature
> than the TestFlight copy of the same bundle id, so iOS refuses to install one
> over the other. The existing app must be deleted first, and **that erases its
> container — notes, sync settings, and the device's SSH key.** Sync from the
> phone first. If the same version is already on TestFlight, install it from
> there instead: that path updates in place and keeps the data.

---

## GitHub Actions release (normal route)

The one-time setup, secrets, and release flow are documented in
[`docs/MOBILE_AD_HOC_GITHUB_ACTIONS.md`](../../docs/MOBILE_AD_HOC_GITHUB_ACTIONS.md).
For a release from `main`:

```sh
git tag mobile-v0.2.7
git push origin mobile-v0.2.7
```

When the **Mobile Ad Hoc** workflow succeeds, open
`https://type-ota.vercel.app` in Safari on a registered device. A manual run is
also available under Actions and accepts an explicit version/build number.

## Local-build prerequisites

- Apple Developer Program membership, team `Y377P5XKGJ`.
- App Store Connect API key at
  `~/.appstoreconnect/private_keys/AuthKey_W2Y52J5N33.p8`
  (issuer `bd0c62da-fcbf-4770-a10d-2ee30da0963e`). Same key CI uses.
  **No local Apple Distribution certificate or `.p12` is needed** — `security
  find-identity -v -p codesigning` on this Mac normally shows only an "Apple
  Development" identity, never "Apple Distribution". That is fine: §1.5's
  archive step only needs *some* valid identity (Development is enough), and
  §1.6's `-exportArchive -allowProvisioningUpdates` is what actually gets the
  Distribution certificate — the API key lets Xcode fetch/provision it from
  App Store Connect during export, without ever touching the local keychain.
  Don't go hunting for a `.p12` or let Xcode create a certificate by hand
  first; just run the documented archive + export commands and let export
  handle it. (Verified 2026-09-04: archived with "Apple Development", the
  exported `.ipa` came back signed "Apple Distribution: Maxim Ignatev
  (Y377P5XKGJ)", and `security find-identity` was unchanged before and after —
  no certificate was created or consumed locally.)
- **The target device's UDID registered in the developer account.** Ad-hoc
  provisioning profiles embed a device list; export fails while building the
  profile if the device is not on it. Get the UDID from Xcode → Window → Devices
  and Simulators (the "Identifier" field), or `xcrun devicectl list devices`,
  and register it at developer.apple.com → Devices.
- Xcode with the iOS SDK, CocoaPods, and a Rust toolchain with the
  `aarch64-apple-ios` target.
- For the Vercel path: `vercel` CLI, logged in (`vercel whoami`).

Run everything from the repo root unless a step says otherwise.

---

## 1. Build the .ipa

### 1.1 Checks

```sh
npm run typecheck -w @typenotes/mobile
npm run test -w @typenotes/mobile
```

### 1.2 Set the version

`apps/mobile/app.config.js` reads `MOBILE_VERSION` and `IOS_BUILD_NUMBER` from
the environment and overrides whatever `app.json` says — that is how CI gets the
version from the tag without a commit. `expo prebuild` bakes those values into
`apps/mobile/ios/Type/Info.plist` as **literals**, not as `$(MARKETING_VERSION)`
references.

That last detail is the trap: passing `MARKETING_VERSION=` /
`CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION=` on the `xcodebuild` command line does nothing,
because `Info.plist` no longer refers to those build settings. An archive built
that way silently carries the old version.

So either re-run prebuild with the environment set:

```sh
cd apps/mobile
MOBILE_VERSION=0.2.6 IOS_BUILD_NUMBER=2026090101 npx expo prebuild --platform ios
```

…or edit the two files by hand and keep them in sync:

- `apps/mobile/app.json` — `expo.version`, `expo.ios.buildNumber`
- `apps/mobile/ios/Type/Info.plist` — `CFBundleShortVersionString`,
  `CFBundleVersion`

`apps/mobile/ios/` is tracked, so inspect the diff after a prebuild. Only use
`--clean` after changing Expo config, plugins, or native dependencies.

### 1.3 Regenerate the Rust core with a device slice

The checked-in `packages/mobile-core/src/index.tsx` is a mock fallback so clean
clones and Expo Go work. A device build needs the real UniFFI turbo module:

```sh
IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=16.4 npm run codegen:ios:device -w @typenotes/mobile-core
```

`codegen:ios` (no `:device`) builds a **simulator-only** slice — it will archive
and then fail to link or run on hardware. Verify the package did not stay in
demo mode:

```sh
test -f packages/mobile-core/TypeCore.podspec
test -f packages/mobile-core/TypenotesMobileCoreFramework.xcframework/ios-arm64/libtype_ffi.a
grep -q 'Generated by uniffi-bindgen-react-native' packages/mobile-core/src/index.tsx
! grep -q '__isDemoCore' packages/mobile-core/src/index.tsx
```

Codegen overwrites `src/index.tsx`, so `git status` will show it modified
afterwards. That is expected — **do not commit it**; restore the fallback with
`git checkout -- packages/mobile-core/src/index.tsx` when done. The file cannot
be gitignored: `package.json` declares it as the package `main`, so a clean
clone without it has no entry point at all.

### 1.4 Pods

```sh
cd apps/mobile/ios
pod install
```

Run it from that directory. `pod install --project-directory=apps/mobile/ios`
from the repo root fails — the `Podfile` resolves React Native's location from
`Dir.pwd`, so it looks for `apps/mobile/node_modules/react-native` and does not
find the hoisted copy.

Confirm `Pods/Target Support Files/Pods-Type/Pods-Type.release.xcconfig`
contains `-lz -liconv`; the `Podfile` post-install hook adds them, and they are
required because `libtype_ffi.a` statically includes libgit2.

### 1.5 Archive

From `apps/mobile/ios`:

```sh
xcodebuild -workspace Type.xcworkspace -scheme Type -configuration Release \
  -destination "generic/platform=iOS" -archivePath build/Type.xcarchive archive \
  DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=Y377P5XKGJ CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Automatic -allowProvisioningUpdates \
  -authenticationKeyPath ~/.appstoreconnect/private_keys/AuthKey_W2Y52J5N33.p8 \
  -authenticationKeyID W2Y52J5N33 \
  -authenticationKeyIssuerID bd0c62da-fcbf-4770-a10d-2ee30da0963e
```

Check the version before spending an export on it:

```sh
/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy \
  -c "Print :ApplicationProperties:CFBundleShortVersionString" \
  -c "Print :ApplicationProperties:CFBundleVersion" \
  build/Type.xcarchive/Info.plist
```

### 1.6 Export ad-hoc

`ExportOptionsAdHoc.plist` is the ad-hoc counterpart to `ExportOptions.plist`
(App Store). `release-testing` is Xcode 15+'s name for the method previously
called `ad-hoc`.

```sh
xcodebuild -exportArchive -archivePath build/Type.xcarchive \
  -exportOptionsPlist ../ExportOptionsAdHoc.plist \
  -exportPath build/export-adhoc \
  -allowProvisioningUpdates \
  -authenticationKeyPath ~/.appstoreconnect/private_keys/AuthKey_W2Y52J5N33.p8 \
  -authenticationKeyID W2Y52J5N33 \
  -authenticationKeyIssuerID bd0c62da-fcbf-4770-a10d-2ee30da0963e
```

### 1.7 Verify the .ipa

Confirm both the version and that the target device made it into the embedded
profile — a profile missing the device produces an "unable to install" that
looks identical to a signing failure:

```sh
cd $(mktemp -d) && unzip -q /path/to/build/export-adhoc/Type.ipa

/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy \
  -c "Print :CFBundleShortVersionString" \
  -c "Print :CFBundleVersion" \
  -c "Print :CFBundleIdentifier" \
  Payload/Type.app/Info.plist

security cms -D -i Payload/Type.app/embedded.mobileprovision > prof.plist
/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy -c "Print :Name" -c "Print :ProvisionedDevices" prof.plist
```

Expect `iOS Team Ad Hoc Provisioning Profile: com.typenotes.mobile` and the
device's UDID in the list.

---

## 2. Distribute over the air

iOS installs a signed build from a plain web page: Safari opens an
`itms-services://` URL, that fetches a manifest, and the manifest points at the
`.ipa`. Both files must come over **HTTPS with a publicly trusted certificate**
— true since iOS 7.1; a self-signed certificate is rejected unless its CA is
installed and explicitly trusted on the device.

This changes delivery only. The build is still ad-hoc signed, so only devices in
the profile can install it.

### 2.1 Generate the site

`scripts/ota.mjs` reads the bundle id, version, and build number out of the
`.ipa` itself rather than from `app.json`, because iOS matches the manifest
against the payload and a `bundle-version` that disagrees makes the install
silently do nothing.

```sh
npm run ota -w @typenotes/mobile -- build \
  ios/build/export-adhoc/Type.ipa \
  --base-url https://type-ota.vercel.app
```

Writes `apps/mobile/ios/build/ota/` (override with `--out`):

| file | |
|---|---|
| `index.html` | landing page with the Install button |
| `manifest.plist` | what `itms-services` fetches |
| `Type.ipa` | the payload |
| `vercel.json` | content types — hosts otherwise guess wrong for `.plist` |

### 2.2 Deploy to Vercel

The manifest needs **absolute** URLs, so the host URL has to be known before
generating. First time round it is not, so deploy twice:

```sh
cd apps/mobile/ios/build/ota
vercel deploy --prod --yes                       # 1. learn the URL
vercel inspect <deployment-url> | grep -A3 Aliases
```

Take the stable alias — for this project, `https://type-ota.vercel.app` — then
regenerate with it and redeploy:

```sh
npm run ota -w @typenotes/mobile -- build \
  ios/build/export-adhoc/Type.ipa --base-url https://type-ota.vercel.app
cd apps/mobile/ios/build/ota && vercel deploy --prod --yes
```

Vercel content-addresses uploads, so the second push of the same 30 MB payload
is near-instant. **Later releases are a single pass** — the alias is stable, so
generate with `--base-url https://type-ota.vercel.app` and deploy once.

The Vercel project name comes from the directory name (`ota` → adjust with
`vercel link` if you want something else). The existing project is `type-ota`
under `maxim-ignatevs-projects-ef3992aa`.

### 2.3 Verify before touching the phone

```sh
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "index: %{http_code} %{content_type}\n"    https://type-ota.vercel.app/
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "manifest: %{http_code} %{content_type}\n" https://type-ota.vercel.app/manifest.plist
curl -sSI https://type-ota.vercel.app/Type.ipa | grep -iE "^HTTP|content-type|content-length"
```

Expect `text/html`, `text/xml`, and `application/octet-stream`. A `401` means
Vercel Deployment Protection is on for the project — turn it off in the
project's settings, or the phone gets a login wall instead of the app.

Also confirm the manifest picked up the right URL and version:

```sh
curl -sS https://type-ota.vercel.app/manifest.plist | grep '<string>'
```

### 2.4 Install

Open `https://type-ota.vercel.app` **in Safari on the device** and tap Install.
Other browsers ignore the `itms-services` scheme and the button does nothing.
The icon appears on the home screen with a progress ring; the first launch may
need Settings → General → VPN & Device Management to trust the developer.

The URL is public — anyone can download the binary, though only registered
devices can install it. Delete the Vercel project when done if that matters.

---

## 3. Alternative: local server behind a tunnel

For a one-off install with nothing left hosted anywhere:

```sh
npm run ota -w @typenotes/mobile -- serve ios/build/export-adhoc/Type.ipa
# in another shell:
cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8787     # or: ngrok http 8787
```

Open the tunnel's HTTPS URL in Safari. The server generates the manifest per
request from the `Host` / `X-Forwarded-Proto` headers, so the public URL does
not have to be known in advance and nothing needs regenerating when the tunnel
comes up with a fresh address. Neither tunnel client is installed by default
(`brew install cloudflared`).

## 4. Alternative: cable

Xcode → Window → Devices and Simulators → select the device → drag the `.ipa`
into "Installed Apps", or use Apple Configurator. No HTTPS, no hosting; the
device has to be connected and unlocked. Note that AirDropping an `.ipa` or
opening it from Files does **not** work — iOS will not install it that way.

---

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| Export fails building the provisioning profile | device UDID not registered in the account |
| Install button does nothing | page opened in a browser other than Safari |
| "Unable to install" | device not in the embedded profile (§1.7), or a differently-signed copy of the same bundle id is already installed |
| Install starts, then the icon greys out permanently | manifest `bundle-identifier` / `bundle-version` disagree with the payload |
| Safari shows the manifest as text | host served `.plist` with the wrong content type — `vercel.json` fixes this on Vercel |
| Phone gets a Vercel login page | Deployment Protection enabled on the project |
| App launches into demo mode with a banner | `codegen:ios:device` was skipped, or `src/index.tsx` was reverted before archiving (§1.3) |
| Crash on launch on device only | simulator-only core slice — `codegen:ios` instead of `codegen:ios:device` |

Replace TestFlight mobile release pipeline with ad-hoc distribution

TestFlight review latency was blocking fast device testing. mobile-adhoc.yml

publishes it as a workflow artifact and GitHub Release asset, and deploys an

Add local sync checkpoints

Expose an offline commit operation through the shared Rust core, desktop Tauri commands, and mobile FFI bridge.

Add checkpoint buttons to both sync UIs and preserve local checkpoint history when it is later pushed.

=== dff79aa9 ===
Fix vitest failing on notes-store.test.ts's real react-native/expo-file-system imports

sync-store.ts now imports diagnostics-store.ts (for the sync-log capture
toggle), which notes-store.ts already imported transitively - pulling
expo-file-system/legacy into notes-store.test.ts's module graph for the
first time. Its "default" export resolves to raw, untranspiled TS that

=== da205b41 ===
Fix Iroh audio archive hangs and split mobile sync into notes-then-audio phases

Recording upload had no timeout anywhere in its network path (the offer ack
read, the desktop's blob fetch, the pairing check), so a stalled relay/NAT
path hung indefinitely — and because prepareAudioForPush ran before every
git push/pull, one stuck recording blocked notes from syncing at all. Each
network step now runs under a bounded timeout and failures are per-recording
(skip and retry next sync) instead of aborting the whole archive.

Mobile sync now runs notes first: push/pull no longer wait on the audio
archive, which runs fire-and-forget afterward under its own state
(audioArchiveState) so a slow/failed recording transfer can never again read
as "syncing forever" with no notes arriving.

Also adds an opt-in, timestamped sync-log capture + export (Settings ->
Diagnostics) so a stuck sync can be diagnosed from a standalone/TestFlight
build with no attached console.

Bump mobile to 0.2.13 (2026090402).

=== 9db67e20 ===
Move the native back band to what the trace measured

The first on-device trace showed the 0.7 split never protected the gesture it
exists for: its bottom is 652pt on a 932pt screen, and every recorded swipe up
started at y>=499 — inside the band, contested by the native pop. The back
swipes stopped at y=474, so the two gestures do separate by height, just around
the middle of the screen. NATIVE_BACK_BAND_FRACTION -> 0.52.

Three trace defects made the readout hard to trust, all fixed:

- onFinalize fires twice for a handed-over touch (once when manager.fail()
  resolves the handler, again when the finger lifts), so every "back" row was
  recorded twice. Guarded with traceEmitted.
- maxDy stopped growing at activation, because RNGH stops delivering
  onTouchesMove once a handler activates. It read as though no swipe up ever
  travelled past 33pt. maxPull, taken from onUpdate, records the real travel.
- "released" lumped together a pull the user did not finish and a drag taken
  back from us mid-flight. Split out as "cancelled" (onEnd with success=false).

Rows now also print band/free, since the same outcome means different things
inside and outside the band.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/REDACTED
Entire-Checkpoint: 0590bbd7e7b6

=== 03a0923a ===
Zone the capture screen instead of racing the native back gesture

The swipe up to file mostly did not register, and two previous rounds of
threshold tuning did not help because thresholds were never the problem.

react-native-screens' full-screen pop recognizer is a bare
UIPanGestureRecognizer with no direction check (RNSScreenStack.mm:166-170).
gestureRecognizerShouldBegin looks at nothing but where the touch started
(:812-885) and calls cancelTouchesInParent on begin, so it wins on ~10pt of
movement in any direction — including straight up — and kills our touch. The
two libraries cannot negotiate: each returns NO for the other in every
simultaneity and failure delegate, and RNGH's simultaneousWithExternalGesture
silently drops a recognizer with no handler tag.

gestureResponseDistance is the one lever that works, because it decides before
the drag begins. Capture is now split by height: above the line the native
interactive pop is untouched, below it — where a thumb starts pushing the page
up — the native recognizer is never offered the touch and the swipe up is
uncontested. A decisive rightward drag down there pops from the screen itself,
same native animation.

That makes manager.fail(), which is terminal for the whole touch, worth its
cost only inside the native band. Everywhere else the gesture declines to
activate and keeps watching.

Filing also stopped blocking the next touch. It waited up to
COMMIT_HANDOVER_MS for storage before showing the fresh page, holding
`transitioning` — and therefore killing every touch — for up to 1.6s, so
swiping again right after a swipe that "didn't work" was guaranteed to fail
too. The fresh session is installed before anything is awaited, so the blank
page can come in at once.

Adds a Gesture trace behind Settings -> Diagnostics (off by default, one
runOnJS hop per touch, in-memory only) so the band line and the thresholds can
be moved from evidence rather than from mechanics.

apps/mobile/GESTURES.md records the whole investigation, including the two
rejected alternatives — driving the back transition ourselves behind a Menu
replica, and react-native-screens' goBackGesture — and why each was turned
down, so the decision can be revisited without redoing the research.
